utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue the examination of the present witness, I'd like to inform the parties that the Chamber got copies of a letter of Mr. Ierace to the Defence of the 30th of October, 2002 in response of a telefax message of 30th October 2002 from Ms. Pilipovic, which contains a list of Defence exhibits. The Prosecution is right that such a list of exhibits should indicate through which witness the documents will be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you render any decision, we have scrupulously followed the procedure requested in this morning, the letter in response to the Prosecutor. And before you give us the decision, we wanted you to know what our response to the Prosecutor was, that is, that there was a correspondence in the night. The letter was addressed directly to the number given for Ms. Kelly Philpott. And I checked it this morning. The response is somewhere in the organisation, but I don't know how this letter can be delivered. We sent it in the night and it didn't arrive. So I want to be a messenger and maybe bring the letter myself but that would be a waste of time. So there is a response dated the 30th. It's extremely detailed. And before you render any decision, we just wanted you to have a look at the response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I remind the Defence that if faxes are sent over in the night that hard copies are available for the Chamber in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you could perhaps have a hard copy during the break. This is something that I could do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if faxes are sent overnight -- and the Chamber highly appreciates the efforts made by the Defence even to work at night -- but then in order to be fully informed, the Chamber would like to receive hard copies the next morning so that we at least can read them, and we'll read them during the first break. We'll leave then the issue until -- until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at the same time, the Registry will try to see whether the fax could be retrieved at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would also appreciate hard copy faxes in that situation, particularly if Mr. Piletta-Zanin faxes it to the Registry. As a large organisation, a fax that is sent to the Registry might take two days before it reaches OTP in the course of the internal mail system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence does as much as it can to fax at the same time to the Prosecutor and to what we call the senior legal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... wait until we have received copies. It's not a matter on which we should waste time in court. The Chamber will look at the response, and then we'll decide when and where this exchange of information needs further attention. Whether this would be in court or whether this would be at a 7.30 morning meeting. Mr. Usher, the witness is standing by, I take it. Could you please escort him into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, I do understand that you can hear me in a language you can understand. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you'll be further examined by counsel for the Defence. Mr. Piletta-Zanin..

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yesterday we broke during the question about the areas that you mentioned, zones like Grbavica, Ilidza, et cetera. Referring to those areas that you mentioned, were these areas in some way enclosed? That is, were people able to leave normally regarding the war conditions and so on? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since these areas were enclosed, were surrounded, the movement was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd like to come back more in detail on the Lukavica area. You knew this area. From the site of the Lukavica barracks, what could one see looking in the direction of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are able to see the roofs of buildings in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Which Dobrinja are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talk about Dobrinja IV.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Dobrinja IV? And that is in the Serb part that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was one able to see even further?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the distance you could see a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. From the top floor of the Lukavica barracks, was it possible to specifically see just behind the very first line of the buildings in Dobrinja IV which is under Serb control; yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, witness - I'm sorry - I'd like to come back to two matters with respect to the destructions in Sarajevo in general. According to what you personally know about the facts, could you tell us when - and I mean during which period in general - was it that the major part of destruction of buildings occurred during this war. Was it the beginning, middle, or the end?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think by the end of 1992 and beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I am now going to come back to cultural facilities. Do you know about high-ranking cultural facilities like religious buildings, mosques, that were targeted and destroyed in the part of Sarajevo that remained in the hands of the BH side?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you were in Lukavica, you said that you were able to travel to two or three areas, like Grbavica, like Ilijas and so on -- sorry, Ilidza, I meant. Were you able to see the city from these areas, the city -- part of the city that remained under the control of the BH side?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were able to see the first buildings on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Were you able to see the areas where the mosques were?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were these minarets up? Were they standing?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have knowledge of any churches, whatever they were, Orthodox, Catholic, or even Protestant churches that were shelled by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serb forces; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us which company -- you've told us that you were a military police officer. Which company were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the Battalion Military Police at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps -- or with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this the 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the 4th Military Police Battalion broken down into companies, military police companies?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many companies were in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many companies were in the battalion during the time period that you were a member of the 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which of these three companies were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the period from September 1992 through August 1994, did you remain throughout that period in the 1st Company?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What rank did you personally hold during that time period?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of your company commander during this time period?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't paying attention -- pardon me. I was inattentive, but I believe that the testimony of this person consisted of saying that he stayed with the army in Sarajevo until October 1993, I believe. He said yesterday, and we can certainly find the place -- so asking the question until -- where he was until August 1994, it seems to be the result of an erroneous reading, or perhaps this question would not be acceptable as it is asked with reference to chronology. So perhaps the Prosecutor could tell us where did he stay until August 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- it's not my recollection. I don't know, Mr. Mundis, whether you have in your mind that the witness testified that he was only during a limited period in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask that before I say anything further that the witness remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please take off your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I recall the witness yesterday testifying about events up to 1993 but I don't recall the Defence specifically asking him beyond that time period where he was or what he was doing, in the first instance. In the second instance, I think the question that I put to the witness was quite clear. His answer was quite clear. He offered no clarification or correction to the question that I posed to him. And number three, again, Mr. President, the Prosecution would submit that the comments just made by Mr. Piletta-Zanin were inappropriate in the witness's presence with the witness wearing his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what would have been appropriate if you would be right - we'll check that - would be that the question would misrepresent the testimony of the witness and would therefore be inadmissible and then you would have had to ask the witness to take off his headphones and then you could have pointed to in what respect in your view the testimony was misrepresented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do want to assist Mr. Mundis because yesterday in line 5 of page 4006 this witness said the following: [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ... until the 17th of October, 1993." [Interpretation] Which means that he stayed in Lukavica until the 17th of October, 1993. That is clear. And if he's asked questions about afterwards, then that there are certain -- some questions about some procedural ambushes, because that's the reason why we're objecting, hoping that we will be understood properly as that there will be no comments on the fact that the Defence has a right to make objections certainly when they are founded, as they are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether the objections are founded is for the Chamber to decide, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We'll first check what it is. The testimony of -- about the 17th of October is about his stay in Lukavica. It does not say that much on what happened after the 17th of October. Perhaps that could be clarified. But the testimony was not that the witness was not somewhere in or near Sarajevo after the 17th of October. It says that he was until the 17th of October in Lukavica. Perhaps you could clarify the issue, Mr. Mundis. That would be better than to spend more time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I allowed -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, I'm not in agreement with this because I -- Mr. President, I just will allow myself to say that the question is in reference to the 1st Company. Of course the 1st Company that was in Sarajevo, in Lukavica. And if the witness said, "I left Lukavica," he then necessarily -- there was a link in Mr. Mundis's question. It was linked to the 1st Company. I think that was very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I allowed Mr. Mundis to clarify the issue. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the time period from September 1992 through August 1994, did you remain a private with the 1st Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an ordinary soldier in the company of military police until the 17th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what did you do after the 17th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to my city, where I worked at the commission for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After the 17th of October --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid. The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, is it your testimony that after the 17th of October, 1993, you were demobilised?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left because -- for medical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So approximately 17 October 1993 you were medically discharged from the VRS. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the 4th Military Police Battalion of the SRK, which you were assigned to until the 17th of October, 1993, that battalion reported directly to the corps commander, General Galic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So the battalion commander reported directly to General Galic.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To whom did the battalion commander report directly?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I to say the name? Should I say the name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what answer to expect, if there would be any reason to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We can certainly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President -- Mr. President, the problem that we want to raise here is the problem of factual matters. This witness said that he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, does the witness have to take his headphones off? Yes. Could you please take your headphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What we want to do is to respect the usual procedure that you imposed on the parties, that is, that we check if this witness who was an ordinary soldier, that is, a private without a rank, has the necessary competence to state matters regarding the hierarchy and the structure of the army. That is, did he know very well what type --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as you usually, I would say, we have to lay a factual foundation. The witness's answer to two questions, the first that the presiding commander did not directly report to General Galic, which suggested he had some knowledge. And the answer to the second question was that he said, "Am I to say the name? Should I say the name," which suggests that this witness would even know about that person. So there's no reason at this moment to lay a further foundation as far as his factual knowledge is concerned, because it appears from his answers. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can go into private session if there's any specific reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if you know, approximately how many military police officers or soldiers or -- the total strength of the 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an exact figure, but I would say around 90 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: 90 men for the entire battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many men were in the 1st Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 1st Company, of which I was a member, there were 35 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the specific roles and duties of the 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific duties were to provide security for the command, escort of convoys, and patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned yesterday an investigative role and a policing role; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the specific powers or authority that you as a military police officer were vested with?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically my duties were linked to logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were with the 1st Military Police Company, did you receive any type of training as a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of training did you receive?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went through basic police training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did that consist of?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any training on military law or military regulations?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any training on how to make an arrest of someone?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have training on how to restrain an individual either during the course of that arrest or after that person had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any specialised firearms training as part of that military police training?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any training with respect to investigative techniques?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any specialised training in any kind of forensic evidence collection?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the time period that you were part of the 1st Military Police Company, were any members of that company, to your knowledge, used in a combat role?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently during the time period that you were with the 1st Military Police Company were members of that unit used in a combat role?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall in which specific areas members of your company were used in combat roles?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which areas those members were used in combat roles.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the locations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention Dobrinja IV, Pecinica, Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to Dobrinja IV, do you recall the approximate time period in which military police forces were used in combat roles?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Dobrinja IV?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was the end of June 1992 when the first operation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if they were so used in that role at any other time in Dobrinja IV?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only operation of any size during the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned Pecinica. Do you recall approximately what time period or time periods military police forces were used in a combat Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. role in that area?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was that the only time period those forces were used in Pecinica?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us at what other time periods such forces were used in Pecinica.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When was that, witness?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly, but I think it was July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn now to Grbavica. Do you recall the specific date or time period when military police units were used in a combat role in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the 4th Military Police Battalion used a four-wheeled armoured vehicle known as a BOV as their standard vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time period that you were assigned to the 4th Military Police Battalion, were the three companies that comprised that battalion assigned to specific areas?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, could you repeat that answer. I missed the first part.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was the 1st Military Police Company assigned to - which area or areas - during the time period you were with that unit?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Company was assigned to the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the 2nd Military Police Company, if you know, where was that unit assigned?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was assigned to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the 3rd Military Police Company, where was that assigned?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Military Police Company was also assigned to the barracks in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So two of the battalion's three companies were at Lukavica barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, witness, if you know, approximately how many personnel were assigned to the 3rd Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was it approximately the same size as the 1st Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the military --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hesitated for a long time, but I have the impression that all these questions about the size of the company, the number of soldiers, the reinforcements, it is hard to establish any relevance to the facts. This man was a soldier of a particular company. He has told us what he knows. I don't think that the size of the companies is so very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take your headphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the witness be excused from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would ask him to leave the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just for the record, I asked that the witness be escorted out because it seemed to me from where I was standing that the witness was able to read the transcript on the screen as I was asking him questions. Mr. President, in the first place -- at the first instance let me also put on the record that the 65 ter summaries that we received with respect to this witness, as well as the expanded 65 ter statements, made no reference whatsoever to the fact that this witness was a member of a military police unit. Obviously, in any kind of case where we're dealing with, in particular, Article 7(3) responsibility of an accused, and we've got a military police person present, the Prosecution would submit that anything going to the enforcement of the law is certainly of relevance, and that goes to reports, investigations that may have been conducted, disciplinary proceedings that may have been initiated, whether or not the military police were sent out to arrest anyone, on the basis of such charges, and given the fact that we had no notice whatsoever that this witness was a member of a military police unit, in our respectful view, would -- well, first of all, we believe that this evidence is relevant. But second of all, I believe that I should be given some leeway to expand upon the military police and the role of those people in general simply because we didn't have advance notice that this witness was even a member of such a unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether the whole structure then of the units this witness was serving in are that relevant, but the Chamber also noticed yesterday that the Defence asked questions about whether investigations were known to this witness as a member of a police unit, and the summary does not say one single word about this witness serving on a police unit. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Perhaps -- or rather, certainly that is right. But that is not the problem. The problem is that questions are being put about the size of the companies, and that is why I am objecting, Mr. President. It's not against anything else. It is the size that bothers us, the strength of the companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could, Mr. President. The evidence that we've adduced thus far in the course of this trial is that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps consisted of between 17 -- or approximately 17 to 18 thousand soldiers. This witness has told us that the Military Police Battalion that was assigned to that corps consisted of approximately 100 men, one-third of whom were at Pale, two-thirds of whom were at Lukavica barracks. It is certainly relevant in the Prosecution's submission that of the approximately 70 men, 70 military police officers that were available to the accused at Lukavica barracks, would certainly have relevance to his ability to police and patrol those forces that were under his command. We're talking about 70 military policemen being responsible for the law enforcement of 17 to 18 thousand troops over a very widespread confrontation line, and that certainly is relevant as far as the Prosecution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied to the extent that the availability and the strength of the police units within the SRK are of some relevance, Mr. Mundis, but the Chamber would invite the Prosecution then to also elicit from the witness whether this was the only police force or at least that we have to -- I mean, a number might be relevant, but then of course it should be established as well whether this was the entire available police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's exactly where I was intending to go, Mr. President. And leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom again. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just have to explain to you that if there is any procedural issue to be discussed between the parties, it's sometimes better that the witness would not follow it because it might influence him and the exchange of views of the parties should be kept away from a witness. That's the reason why we asked you to leave the courtroom. But the matter has been settled and we'll continue now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the time period up until your medical discharge in October 1993, did the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps have one military police battalion, that is, the 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So all of the corps' military police resources were in that one battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the two companies, that is, the 1st Company and the 3rd Company, that were at Lukavica barracks, those two companies were responsible for military police duties throughout the region covered by this Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like the record to reflect that again I can hear noises from the other side of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't hear it through my earphones -- at least, I heard something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, once again the Prosecution is saying something that is not true. We didn't say anything. I was just writing. Maybe the pen scratching the paper. What did I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Galic -- General Galic did you try to draw the attention of counsel? Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that I did wish to draw the attention of my counsel, not as loudly as Mr. Mundis seems to think, but it is true, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any need to confer with counsel, perhaps you -- perhaps you'd do it even louder and say "Mr. President" or something like that, so that I know that you need to confer with counsel and that no misunderstandings will come up. So it was not a scratching of your pen, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and it was heard by the Prosecution. Whenever you need to confer with counsel, General Galic, please say it as loud as possible if -- to me, and then I'll stop the examination of the witness and I'll give you an opportunity to do so. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. But Mr. Piletta-Zanin didn't hear me. If he had heard me, he would have turned around. So it's my mistake. I do apologise. I usually say something very quietly. May I? I say it very quietly or I ask you for your permission to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you allow me, and so long as it won't upset the Prosecution, I would like to confer with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, to your knowledge, did each of the brigades within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps also have a military company assigned to that brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in the 1st Military Police Company of the 4th Military Police Battalion, that is, your unit, whom did you receive your orders from?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received orders from our superior, and that was the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know whom the company commander received his orders from? Would that be the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm aware that you at some point became responsible for the logistics within your unit. Can you remind me approximately when that was that you assumed responsibility for the logistics.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took over responsibility at the beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So throughout the period from June 1992 through October 1993 your responsibilities were in the area of logistics within your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you were injured approximately on the 1st of July, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, objection. I should like to know where with precision this witness said that he had been wounded or injured, the word used by the Prosecution. I would like the exact spot to be indicated for me in the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm simply asking the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but the witness never said that he had been injured, so I'd like to be told where he said so in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You -- Mr. Mundis, you asked the witness -- I think you injured approximately on the 1st of July, 1993; is that right? That's what you asked the witness. That suggests, of course -- leading questions are not inadmissible during the -- during cross-examination. On the other hand, if there would be serious reasons to believe that the medical situation of the witness would not be due to any injuries, then -- but I'm not clear in my recollection whether the witness said something about that yesterday. But it's -- I mean, it's not very -- it's not of great assistance to create this kind of confusion and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness you told us you were medically discharged on the 17th of October, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were your military duties between the 1st of July, 1993 and the time you were medically discharged on the 17th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just perhaps assist the parties. Yesterday the witness said: "In Lukavica I was an ordinary soldier and as I had been hurt, injured, I was relieved of certain activities, so I mainly worked in logistics and I did guard duty." Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the objection was --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not going to discuss any more about this. But you wanted to have the source of the injuries. I gave it to you. I don't know whether it corresponds exactly, but it's page 14609. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I allowed Mr. Mundis --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our rights have been offended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to proceed. And just before the break, I'll give you an opportunity to respond. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you said after the 1st of July, 1993 that you were just an ordinary soldier. Does that mean an ordinary soldier in the military police -- the 1st Military Police Company or were you no longer assigned to that unit after July 1st, 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just an ordinary soldier in that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the 1st Military Police Company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the time that you were assigned to the 1st Military Police Company, do you know if that unit received orders to conduct investigations?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigations were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, witness, during the time you were with the 1st Military Police Company, did that company have regular training meetings or weekly meetings where all the members of the unit were brought together?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings were mostly held once a fortnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the course of those meetings, were you provided with updates and general information about what was -- the unit was -- what mission the unit was undertaking?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you also have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to stop for a moment because the LiveNote is not functioning well. I do understand that the interpreters -- technical problems have been solved. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you also, witness, during the time you were with the 1st Military Police Company discuss with other members of that unit the type of work that they were doing?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of offences were most prevalent during the time you were with the 1st Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently that would be detention, one to two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For what kind of crimes would people be detained for one or two days?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly being late from -- when returning from home or drunkenness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently, to your recollection, was drunkenness an issue for someone being arrested?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any specific incidents involving drunkenness? Do any of them come to mind?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe, witness, you testified yesterday about drunk soldiers being on the line, and I believe you were -- you were asked if it happened that soldiers would get intoxicated, and you answered that there were cases. Do you recall any cases where soldiers who were on the front lines were arrested for being intoxicated?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be removed from their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently do you recall that being the case, that someone was removed for drunkenness?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases but not so frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In any of the instances that you recall someone being removed for drunkenness, do you recall whether there were any allegations that those individuals had shot at civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any instances involving soldiers who were intoxicated and had allegedly fired artillery pieces or mortar pieces at civilians due to their intoxication?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You don't recall hearing anything like that; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether during the time you were with the 1st Military Police Company anyone was arrested for violating an order?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How was information concerning the arrests reported up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were given the information by the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question to make it a little more clear. If a member of your company arrested a soldier, what would they do with that soldier? Where would they take them?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be brought to the barracks, where an interview would be held with him, and there would be investigation conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in some instances I assume the investigation would lead to some kind of charges being preferred against an individual?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Some of the individuals who were arrested were then investigated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And on the basis of the investigation, were some of those people then charged with crimes?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't remember any instance where anyone that your unit arrested was ever charged -- formally charged with an offence?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall during the time period that your company was at Lukavica barracks whether there were any kind of court martials or disciplinary proceedings that were held while you were there?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no court martial in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, witness, if you know, a little bit about the relationship between the infantry and artillery soldiers in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the military police.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did the soldiers who were on the front line and the military police have a good relationship? Was there a good relationship between those two types of troops?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship was good, relatively good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware in November of 1992 about incidents where morale between the military police and the front line units was particularly strained?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of an incident in which two soldiers were killed and two soldiers were wounded by a military police BOV as a result of the negligence of one of the gunners in that military police vehicle?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what was the most serious crime that you can remember being investigated by your military police company during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever -- did your unit ever to your knowledge investigate anyone for sniping at civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did anyone in your unit investigate anyone for firing artillery or mortars at civilians?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall during the time you were present whether your unit investigated anyone -- any SRK soldiers for murdering other SRK soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the time that you were in a military police -- in the 1st Military Police Company, did you ever see any kind of weapon that might be characterised as a sniper weapon? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you see, if you know the make of that weapon?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an army rifle with a sniper sight, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this just one rifle that you saw or was it more than one?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where you saw this sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is, in the company headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the company headquarters building is located or was located at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What -- based on your military police training, what use would a military police company have for a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no special training for snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know where the corps commander's office was located on the Lukavica barracks facility?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was the corps commander's headquarters in relation to the 1st Military Police Company headquarters where you saw the sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In another building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far were those two buildings from one another?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a street between them, perhaps 5, 6 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, to your knowledge, during the time that you were with the 1st Military Police Company, did the corps commander ever visit your headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time period that you were with the 1st Military Police Company at Lukavica barracks, did the corps commander, General Stanislav Galic, ever visit that building to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see the corps commander in your military company's -- military police company headquarter building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from anyone that General Galic had been in your building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see a photograph of General Galic that was taken during a visit to your building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the time that you were stationed at Lukavica barracks, did you ever personally enter the corps commander's office?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever go into the corps command headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For what purpose did you enter that building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was guarding the entrance to the building. I was on guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While you were standing guard duty, did you ever see the accused, General Galic, enter that building or -- did you also see him exit the building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently did you stand guard duty?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One shift, so one shift out of 24 hours -- eight hours out of 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many eight-hour shifts do you recall doing at guard duty outside the command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: More than five?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I couldn't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give me an approximation? Was it 5 times, 10, 15, 20?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you stood guard duty outside the building, did you also have the opportunity to go inside that building?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where inside the building did you go?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There were several or quite a few offices in that building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you enter any of those offices?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which office did you go?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the senior officer under whom was the command of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we may have to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could try to do that in approximately 15 minutes, which would result in approximately the same time used by the Prosecution as the Defence used in the examination-in-chief. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I raise something briefly before we adjourn for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we'll first ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll resume in approximately half an hour, Mr. Vukovic, so -- And before giving you the opportunity, Mr. Ierace, I promised Mr. Piletta-Zanin that he would get an opportunity to respond to an earlier event in this courtroom. But before giving you the opportunity, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I perhaps first will inform you of the following: You asked about a reference of injuries or being injured that was contained in a question of the Prosecution. It took us some time to try to find out what was the factual basis of that. Mr. Mundis then reformulated his question. He Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. didn't rely upon that question any more. I then gave you a source where the witness testified that he was injured. I did that as an indication on how easy it was to retrieve that. And when you further wanted to discuss that, I stopped you because since Mr. Mundis had reformulated his question, there was no need for any further discussion of the issue as such. But you -- I told you that you would have an opportunity to make whatever submission you'd liking to do in that respect. You'll get one minute for that. We'll hear in that minute whether you need more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The reason is very simple: Mr. Mundis's question was, "So you were injured approximately on the 1st of July, 1993." That's page 24, line 8. "Is that correct?" Very well. Now, before that the previous question was on page 24, line 6, "So throughout the period when you were -- from June to October 1993, you remember assigned to logistics; is that correct?" Very well. Now, Mr. President, you reasoned to tell us that on page 14609 the witness did give an answer but he gave an answer about his injury when I asked the question regarding his evacuation from the Viktor Bubanj barracks. So I said, "From the moment when you were evacuated, what happened?" And then he said, in answer, "Since I was injured --" and he was referring to his treatment in the prison where he was. "Because I was injured, I had been injured, I was assigned to the logistics." So the chronology was extremely clear. From the moment when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what you're doing now is to explain why your objection was justified. As I told you before, there was no further need to discuss this matter because Mr. Mundis reformulated his question. You didn't say anything about chronological order. You said, "Where did the witness say that he was injured? Could you tell me whether he said that." Well, he was talking about injuries, and I think the matter has been solved. Then there's no further need to discuss that matter because by reformulating Mr. Mundis well, made the issue a relevant one and we could proceed. And what you are telling us now I think is not a matter that should be pursued any further. You take it that you're entitled to ask to the injuries. I told you where he talked about the injuries. You think that your objection was -- at least your request was justified. I'm not going to rule on that. It's just the matter became irrelevant because Mr. Mundis proceeded in another way and I informed you where you could find the word "injury" and that's what you asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I just wanted to say very clearly was that the Defence believes that the principle of equitable trial is no longer respected when we make an objection and when we're treated in this way, we believe that there is a lack of balance. That's what I'm saying. And this is a very pertinent example. That's what I just said, and I have to say it for the purpose of General Galic's defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Always, if an objection is based on the formulation of a question and if the other party reformulates the question in such a way that the objection is not valid any more - and that's what Mr. Mundis did - then the question has become irrelevant for the further proceedings. But the Chamber has of course listened carefully to your submissions at this moment. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In relation to the next witness, I would be grateful if the Defence could indicate at some stage in the next hour or so whether they believe they have provided us with further expansion of the 65 ter summary since that which was provided to us on the 13th of October, 2002. I make that request because there have been a number of letters which we have received from the Defence in French, including this morning, and the issue is that in the letter of the 13th of October, the Defence indicated that witness would give evidence relevant to five different scheduled sniping incidents and there is no detail at all as to what that evidence is. So the first step is to clarify whether the Defence says it has given us further information. I thought if I made that request at this stage before the break, ultimately it might save time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or is it contained in the overall? Because we received a large set of newly formulated 65 ter summaries. Is it in there, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, or where could the Prosecution find the extended summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to admit I understand this no longer. I addressed a full letter, which you must have seen by now. There was all the data and information that you can imagine. And I don't know whether Mr. Ierace is speaking about this letter, whether he's had a translation, although it is written in the language of the Tribunal. I no longer know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is quite simple, whether any further extended summary after the summary provided on the 13th of October has been provided and where to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wrote this letter I don't know when. Let me find it. But I think it must have been in October. I don't have the document before me. I mean, if the Prosecution had telephoned me to ask me, I would have told them immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend more time on it. This is merely a very practical matter. I'd like to see the parties in five minutes in a room that will be reported to you by the registrar. We'll find a room, and we'll discuss this very practical matter in five minutes. We'll adjourn until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is happy that at least we solved some of the practical problems during the break and we can now continue the cross-examination of the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I have just a couple of follow-up questions from a subject we discussed earlier. When your military police company was investigating someone for serious crimes and there were grounds to proceed, that is, for the investigation to go further than your unit was capable of handling, would a military prosecutor become involved at some point in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were with the 1st Military Police Company, do you remember any instance in which a military prosecutor became involved in the investigation of a crime?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a precise answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by the answer, witness. Do you recall a military prosecutor ever becoming involved or not?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier, witness, that for some of the minor offences the soldier or soldiers would be detained for one or two days. Where did that detention take place?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a detention area within the barracks compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that's within the Lukavica barracks compound? You had a military brig?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, witness, yesterday that you were responsible for logistics within your unit and that one of the important orders that your unit received was to conserve ammunition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, witness, as a means of conserving ammunition, one way of doing that would be to use one or two bullets instead of 100 or 200; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When people were assigned to a task, ammunition was issued to them. It wasn't used before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, witness, but the question is: The fewer bullets used for any particular mission or operation, the fewer bullets that were used would result in conservation of those scarce ammunition resources; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, the standard issue assault rifle used within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was the Kalashnikov; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that weapon has three modes with respect to the trigger: The safety mode, the single-shot mode, and the automatic mode; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as we need to be very precise and we know there are several types of Kalashnikovs - there are Akas and others - I think that we need to specify exactly type of rifle we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you: You answered a question about Kalashnikovs. What Kalashnikov did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind an automatic rifle that was used by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you had in mind as well, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, again, in light of the fact that this weapon had one safety mode and two firing modes, the single-shot mode would conserve the most ammunition; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So if you were attempting to save ammunition and you were faced with a military target such as a machine-gun nest, you might use that weapon in the single-shot mode to attempt to take out that machine nest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid the question isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you were attempting to take out a military target such as a machine-gun nest and you wanted to conserve ammunition, since that was your order, you would use that weapon in the single-shot mode in order to save ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object to this question. The phrase as it was formulated implies that it was his order to save on ammunition, and it appears that this witness was in a combat situation, as we are talking about an attack on a machine-gun nest. If we're talking about that, we have to know what particular situation we are referring to, or is this a hypothetical question, because he's certainly not a strategist regarding attacks on machine-gun nests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, the question as it is put is -- seems to be of a hypothetical nature. That's what you intended to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could you please answer that question, then. So the question is not about what you did but on whether you would use the single-shot mode if you'd save -- if you'd like to follow orders that would have instructed you to save ammunition as good as possible. Would you then use that single mode, single-shot mode? Is the question clear to you, or is it not clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Mundis, try to formulate the question in such a way that the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll try, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if you were attempting to take out a target and you were also under an obligation to conserve ammunition, you would set the weapon on the single-shot mode in order to conserve ammunition; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if - again, hypothetically - if the target that you were attempting to take out presented a danger using that weapon in the single-shot mode due to the range of the weapon, you might bring in a sniper to take out that target.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Because in fact the tactics involved with sniping require far fewer ammunition resources than using machine-gun fire; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday - and this, for the benefit of the Defence, is in the draft transcript, page 64, lines 15 and 16 - you said the following: "It is well known that Muslims rarely respect agreements reached." Do you remember saying that, witness?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "it is well known," to whom is it well known? To you personally? To a group? To a certain class of individuals? Who knows -- or to whom is it well known that Muslims rarely respect agreements reached?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Experience teaches us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "teaches us that," to whom are you referring? Who is the us?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our army, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That would be the VRS?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your army learn any other -- as you put it, did your experience teach your army anything else about the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're objecting on the basis of relevance. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask the witness be escorted out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If -- if that's needed for your response, we'll ask the witness to be escorted out. The objection is there. I do understand that Mr. Mundis for responding to it -- I'll give you an opportunity to further elaborate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But already for a response, the witness needs to leave the courtroom. If you could indicate why you think it lacks --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Very briefly, simply because the fact that this witness thinks this or that about this or that adversary, what he intimately thinks has strictly nothing to do with what the accused is charged of. And I think this is taking it far too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it goes to bias with respect to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you spend a few more words on the bias you indicated, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness, with respect to the quotation which I just repeated from the witness's testimony, I believe that that provides a basis for exploring the depth of this witness's bias towards Muslims. We've had the witness testify extensively about his interactions with Muslims in the Sarajevo community both prior to the indictment period as well as after the indictment period. And if this witness holds - and I'm -- this is what I'm attempting to explore with the witness, if this witness holds particularly offensive viewpoints with respect to Muslims, that would go to the issue of his credibility with respect to what he's testified about with respect to the other side of the conflict that's involved in this case. So we're -- I'm simply attempting to seek from this witness his viewpoint, his personal viewpoint because that goes to bias, but he's also indicated that this experience has taught, as he characterised it, his army -- the army has learned certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand you well that you say that it's not just his personal bias but since he expressed himself in such a way that it is well known that this might be -- such bias might be established for other persons in the same circumstances as well? Is that what you indicate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's possible. I'm -- it's difficult to ascertain based on one or two questions from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But he has said that this experience had taught the VRS, and so certainly we at least have a community, potentially a community bias that's involved. But I'm most particularly interested in exploring with this witness the extent of this bias.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very briefly, Mr. President, one must always put things in context, and I think that a man who saw one of his officers or maybe several of them being dragged out of an ambulance to be killed in cold blood may believe on the basis of his own experience that that was not respecting the word given. And I think it could -- he could be given the benefit of the doubt because unfortunately he himself saw this very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, two comments in quick response.
