But then at a later stage -- unfortunately, I have to tell you that you have to come back and to answer to the last questions of the Defence and also to answer questions of the Prosecution and perhaps questions of the Bench as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate in the event that it is not possible for this witness to be present for a reasonable time tomorrow morning to allow completion of examination-in-chief. Cross-examination, re-examination, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Later today --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That -- well, either later today or we could at least ask the witness when would be convenient or most convenient over the next few months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We have to try to find out whether there's any alternative from having to ask you to return at a later date. But if we would have to ask you to come back to The Hague again, when would be a time that would be suitable for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The alternative is for you to ask me your questions now, since I'm here. But if you want me to come again, I need to have some 10 days' advance notice because of my work. I've been absent for 25 days already from my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was unaware that you stayed a very, very long time, an unusual long time here in The Hague. I will ask the Registry to keep in close contact with the Victims and Witnesses Unit. I would like to ask the parties to remain -- stand by, if we could finish later this day. I don't know whether there is a courtroom available or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to prevent what happened last time, therefore I am addressing the parties that they be in close contact and the Registry would have to know exactly where they are during the rest of the day, even when -- whether faxing or doing other things. Then we'll adjourn, but it's, therefore, uncertain as to -- for -- as to what moment. It might not be until 9.00 this morning. General Galic, I'm very well aware that this might cause you some inconvenience as well, but we have to try to take into consideration also the interest of the witness who has spent here already a long time. So I really apologise for it, if you'd have to return. But one thing is for certain: I'll make sure that we'll not all be in this courtroom at, let's say, 4.00 or 4.30 and then have to leave again without having continued the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the 30 seconds that I have, I will be at the disposal to everyone whenever necessary. I will give my telephone numbers, as customary. Regards the booth from the Serbian to English, page 70, line 12, JNA was not mentioned. And generally speaking, a convent was mentioned. We should verify whether it is the same thing as the theological faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's what the witness testified several times. It's the same for him. But we'll now adjourn -- perhaps we'll see each other later today. If not, then we have to see each other at a later time. We'll adjourn. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to express its appreciation for all those who made themselves available to continue this afternoon. And I think we are now at the point where we could continue the examination-in-chief of Witness DP8. I take it that the protective measures are effective at this moment. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness DP8, thank you very much for coming back. Everyone tries to do his best to enable you to [redacted] [redacted]. Ms. Pilipovic, I am informed that you need -- that Mr. Piletta-Zanin would need another 15 minutes approximately and that the Prosecution would need a little bit over an hour. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, clearly I can't give an indication at this stage, but it would be at least an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. At least an hour. Let's proceed, and may I ask all the parties to work as efficient as we started this morning. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much. General Galic has told me that he would also associate himself to the gratitude expressed by you and he has asked me to say something at the end of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you be shown very quickly the last exhibit that was on the screen. Madam Usher, will you please put the last exhibit on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I simply wanted you -- and it's not very visible. Could you write this "B" more clearly because we can't see it very well. Could you make the letter "B" more clearly on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you be kind enough to use the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm so sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would you please write out the letter "B" more clearly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, that's fine. Thank you. Will you tell me what was the average height of these barricades that we were referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: They were about 3 metres high.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin in giving the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, please. [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Madam Usher please put the other map -- and as far as this one is concerned, I think it's clear enough. Could you please put the other map, the one we had previously on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this map? Would you please indicate on the map with a black pen the place where the small family homes end, mostly owned by Muslims, that you pointed to earlier on as being to the right of the circle in the middle. Could you please indicate the east end of that group of family homes with a pointer, where they end, in other words. With a pointer, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We are talking of that particular area, yes. Will you show us up to where towards the east -- that is, move the pointer to the right. To the right, that's right. Up to where does this area of small houses go in relation to the relatively higher buildings on the right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Fine. And to the south, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: This area here is full of small houses. This was the separation line. These were houses mostly with Serb inhabitants and here Muslim inhabitants. And there was a school that I think was called Simone Bolivar. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness has circled his pointer around the small black dot which is situated in a plot which appears to be totally empty of any graphic presentations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please take the ruler and could you draw a line roughly from the centre of the circle that we have in the centre of the map right up to point 22, trying to put the ruler exactly against point 22. Draw a line, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I would like you to tell us the height of the buildings appearing on the axis of the line that you have drawn, the one that is closest to point 22, in the direction of the line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: The height of all these buildings here is about six to eight storeys. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, what is the distance -- and the scale is 12:5 -- what is the distance between what is sometimes called a convent and sometimes a faculty of theology and point 22? Can you -- I think that the scale is 12:5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: From this circle?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. From the convent. From the theology faculty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: It's more than 2 kilometres, 100 per cent sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map can be withdrawn. We'd like to give him another map now with the number --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is a map relating to incident 25. I should like to indicate this for the benefit of the Prosecution. That map can be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have another copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have to your right a map relating to incident 25. I'm proceeding on the basis of the principle that you recognise the map. Could you tell us with great precision, point 25 that you can identify on this map, what is the distance, please, between that spot and the closest trenches or military facility -- mobile military facility, that is, even the closest spot where there were soldiers? Could you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question requires the witness to state the distance between the spot and the closest trenches or military facility where there were soldiers with no reference to date and no factual basis being established as to how the witness could answer that question for any particular time as to where the nearest soldiers were. I take it, further, that he refers to ABiH soldiers. The question isn't clear as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you formulate the question in such a way that there could be no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll be glad to. But it is quite clearly a reference to the enemy positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to point 25, specifically, what was the closest building, military building or occupied by soldiers, of the opposing army?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again there is no reference to date. The question seems to be going to a particular incident, which as we know occurred on a particular date. Again, no foundation. Again, no reference to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Mr. President, we don't believe that these buildings moved throughout the war, but I will specify the period I'm referring to. But I think that all these buildings exist and many witnesses have told us that the lines didn't move throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will specify the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, please, for the year 1994, and to be more specific, the month or the summer of 1994, what was the military facility or the place occupied by soldiers that was closest to this spot? That is to say, what is the distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: From point 25 and the first building in Vojnicko Polje where the Muslim trenches were was 15 metres on the outside, the width of one road, and that applied throughout the war, that is, from the period of 1992 until 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. For things to be quite clear and for us to save time, this situation on your part of the line, did it change throughout the period that you were familiar with, that is, from 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were there any other buildings of a military nature close to point 25 at any period of time, including around the end of June 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: The entire Vojnicko Polje was considered by us to be a military stronghold of the Muslim forces. This was the front line for us, and all the buildings behind that were areas from which they could fire from, so the whole of Vojnicko Polje as a district was by us considered to be a military base of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time that I referred to, what was the frequency, the strength of fire? I'm talking about the period of June -- the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: There was shooting almost daily. Sometimes it was more; sometimes less intense. But there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you say "shooting," you mean combat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please point at number 26 on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, the same question regarding the same period of time: What is the distance separating this point, 26, from the closest element of a military nature, whether it be a civilian building used for military purposes or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: About 20 or 30 metres. I can't be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, this building appearing next to "26," was it, as far as you know, partially used by the soldiers of the other army?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to leading questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What can you tell us, witness, about who occupied this building during the war, the building under "26"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. There is no foundation laid yet for the witness to be able to give an opinion as to that. In particular, it hasn't been suggested that the witness lived or visited that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we -- let's just -- should we do this when the witness is listening?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for reminding me of this. We could ask the witness to take off his headphones. We can first ask him whether he speaks English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I suggest the appropriate course always is for the witness to leave the courtroom. When a witness says that he or she doesn't speak English, that doesn't allow for the possibility of some knowledge of English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you. Of course, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, usually you're speaking French.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We can just speak French.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I've noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are aware of that, yes. Of course we can ask the witness to leave the courtroom. We can spend a lot of time on the objection if you say there's a more efficient way of solving it because I'm quite willing to rephrase the question or to put an additional question that, of course, would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could say that in German, but that wouldn't simplify things. Let me go to another question. I could move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please put the headphones up again. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, during the war -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, during the war, could you see whether shots were coming for this or that particular building; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, please place your pointer on the line of buildings in front of 26, just in front of 26. Those buildings, that's right. Those buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you from those buildings see incoming fire, fire opened at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you see from any of your other positions other buildings from which --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: -- fire was coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to finish my sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness should not answer the question but first I'll give you an opportunity to complete your question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. With the headphones on of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you should ask him to take them off as you're speaking French, I take it that -- Could you take off your headphones for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The question was whether the witness was able to see fire that was opened from a second line of buildings, that is, those along point 26. If the witness was able to see that, one could deduce that those buildings were used for military purposes, and that would bring us closer to a point of acquittal, and I think that is the right of the Defence to put such a question without any objection by the Prosecution. If he saw whether fire was coming from in the second row of buildings, he will tell us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the relevance of point 26 is that is where, according to the evidence of a Prosecution witness, a boy aged approximately 13 was shot in the middle of the street. That's the first point. Specifically, the witness is not being asked as to a particular day or even a particular period of time when he observed fire. Secondly, the manner which my learned colleague has approached this is to require the witness to put the end of his pointer generally in a group of what we know to be half a dozen high-rise buildings without specifying which ones, singularly, and inviting him to indicate whether he saw fire coming from those buildings. So again, there is not a proper foundation laid. When did the witness see fire coming from which particular buildings? And even that, of course, overlooks the fact that the incident involved, a boy being shot in the middle of the road, not in a building. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. But Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're invited to be a bit more specific. If you're talking about buildings then perhaps at times refer to a specific building rather than a group of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please put your headphones on again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will need a pointer. I will have to use a pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, please pick up your pointer and will you please indicate the basis of the buildings situating immediately to the east of point number 26. Put your pointer clearly at the bottom of that building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, the other one. More to the right. More to the right. Up. Further up. On point 26, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's it. This row of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the witness is showing the row of buildings which is exactly next to point 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you have occasion to see during the war, first of all, fire being opened or any activity of a belligerent nature, a very close nature coming from that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: This building cannot be seen from Nedzarici, this building here. You can only see these first two buildings and the lateral ones. This one cannot be seen from Nedzarici because these two are protecting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now move on to the next map that we're going to show to this witness. It has to do with incident number 23. And the number it bears is 1776. Witness, you have there a map. Unfortunately the central part is not well reproduced, but do you recognise it nevertheless?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I'd like you to point for us on this map at what was in the area marked by the large triangle, which corresponds to the projectile trajectory, and it is in the centre, the middle of this map, for instance, whether the words "Nedzarici," what was there? Were there any obstacles there, anything precluding the view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: This was the locality of Nedzarici, that is, the houses belonging to Serbs in this whole square.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is showing at the surface covered by the triangle and he's pointing at it with his pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether this area was green?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Well, there were many orchards, fruit orchards here. How shall I put it? Next to the monastery there were also some pine trees. Some of them were 10 to 15 metres tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there trees which were closer to the monastery during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. This was ornamental trees around the gate, around the fence of the -- all around the faculty of theology there were trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know if these trees were felled at some point, for instance, because people needed firewood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "no," does it mean that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: No, they were not felled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd like you now to focus on the destruction of Nedzarici. What can you tell the Chamber about the scale of destruction of the houses there and especially during the period under consideration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: During the war, that is, in 1992 to 1994, I do not think that a single house in Nedzarici or a single structure in Nedzarici, a single built structure went unscathed, that is, was not damaged by projectiles. The building of the theological faculty was also targeted on a number of occasions by the Muslim army and it was shelled at some point, and that is how it was until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you also know about the destruction that took place in other neighbourhoods during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We are now talking of Nedzarici --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to the question. It's an invitation to speculate in its present form.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. Fine. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, witness, to your knowledge, that is, during the war, when did the major part of material destruction happen? I'm talking about buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Well, the destruction for the most part occurred at the time when the Muslim formations attacked Nedzarici, and there were many of them. I mean, there were a number of attacks. They attacked Nedzarici frequently. They fired from all the weapons available to them at Nedzarici so that many buildings were damaged, except that in the centre of Nedzarici there were no military facilities, no military strongholds. There were only civilian houses, that is, detached houses where Nedzarici inhabitants lived, including my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll perhaps come back to this question later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I believe that I heard, Mr. President, a word in the witness's language which I do not see in the transcript but I have to hear it once again. How did that happen? May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're asking the witness to repeat his answer or ...? Since you're appointing -- you're saying that the translation is not complete. Is that what I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that I believe I heard a word which does not figure here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You either have to ask the witness to repeat his answer or continue; one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you gave your answer and when I asked you a question, precisely when, could you please repeat because I think -- which words in Serb did you use with regard to the attacks and the time of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I know that it was a daily occurrence between 1992 and 1994. These attacks happened daily. I also know that on the 8th of December, 1992 there was an attack. And these houses I told you were destroyed. But those were exclusively civilian, that is, civilians were living in them, and there wasn't a single military facility there, because my mother lived in our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will stop you, witness. I will stop you now. Could you please remove your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the word that I believe I heard him say was "in the beginning." That was in the beginning. I believe I heard that word, and it doesn't appear here. No, no. We could ask the witness -- perhaps I could ask him a leading question. I don't know. But he said "before General Galic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see -- I've just lost my transcript on my LiveNote on my --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that you ask the witness whether he used the word "at the outset," "in the beginning." And then we shall know whether that was correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to -- first of all, I have -- my LiveNote is -- yes, it's functioning again. It's functioning again. No. No. I really made a mess out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part of your answer was destructions -- what's -- yes, yes. Of course. Could you please put on your headphones. You said something about the damage done during the attacks on Nedzarici. Could you specify that more in detail in time when these attacks on Nedzarici took place, because it might not be -- the translation of your answer might not have been complete. Did you say anything specific about the time of the attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said specifically that between 1992 to 1994 they happened -- and one date I remember is the 8th of December, because I was likely injured by a fragment of a shell which hit Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will ask for the tape to check it. I will ask for the tape to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, those initial attacks by Muslims that you told us about - and you are talking about 1992 - when in 1992 do you remember that? When in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Throughout 1992 there were frequent attacks of the Muslim army on Nedzarici. There was hardly a day that went by when one could walk around Nedzarici normally, and that is what we did. We didn't move around normally. We went out when the darkness fell and we tried to put up screens, curtains, containers, and whatever so as to be less visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you told us a moment ago about your mother. What can you tell this Chamber, please, about her?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [redacted], and on one occasion - I don't know - a shell fell and she was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was -- the witness pointed at something up on the ELMO to certain places which will be redacted now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the second time today, I must apologise. Earlier I indicated that the relevance of point 26 was, as I understood the questioning of my colleague, the reference to a 13-year-old boy being hit in the middle of the street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you were referring to someone watching television in the flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we will notice that. Yes Please proceed. May I ask -- Mr. Witness, Mr. DP8, may I ask you something? Do you hear me, Mr. DP8? Mr. DP8, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are given -- you are giving rather lengthy answers, and since you indicated that you'd like to return to your home country by tomorrow, please listen very carefully to the questions and answer to that question. If, for example, someone could ask what month was it - say, January or February or whatever month it was - then don't tell us about the whole spring or the whole summer, because otherwise it might take far too much time. And for you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you say -- "tell us about your mother," that's not a question that elicits short answers from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Last question, witness: Do you know civilians who perhaps suffered in Nedzarici during the war, that is, people who were killed, who might have been killed? And if you do, how many of them would that be? Do you know the number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I know -- I can say a hundred per cent there were civilian fatalities in Nedzarici. I know about a dozen instances, and I can give you -- I mean, their name, that is, people who were not with the army, who didn't belong to any military formation, who like my mother lived in Nedzarici and who were wounded or killed in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And they died of what, simply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you here. You were just asked whether you could give a number. That was the question. So say 10 or 20 or 30. And then if there's any further information needed, I'm certain that Mr. Piletta-Zanin will ask for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So an estimate, if you can. If you cannot, just say that you cannot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And those individuals that you knew, what did they die of generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Well, they were hit by bullets, small-calibre bullets, or then again by shells which fell in their vicinity, next to their houses or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP8, you'll now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Might I start off in closed session just for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn in to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question: When you started in the armoured company in September 1992, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: My duties were to be a soldier, to carry out military assignments, and those assignments were to deliver food, breakfast, lunch, dinner to the front line, to pull out the dead and the wounded from the front line of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You've told us that APCs were used for that purpose. Did the APCs have weapons, perhaps guns, mounted somewhere on their top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Apart from the duties of delivering food and pulling out the dead and wounded, what else did the armoured company do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: In Nedzarici there wasn't a great deal of action from the armoured vehicle, because it would be crazy to get onto the APC and fire because it was visible from all the surrounding buildings. The APC could easily be seen and easily hit. So usually it was just the driver who went to carry food. And if we went to fetch a wounded person, one of the nurses would come, and they were accommodated at the theology faculty and she would go to extend first aid to the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you're saying that they were the only functions of your company; is that correct? Food delivery and retrieving the dead and wounded; that's all you did in that company. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Never a shot was fired in anger from the guns on the three APCs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I didn't understand quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you telling us that the three guns on the APCs were never used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I didn't say that we had guns on those armoured vehicles. There weren't any guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot assist you since my lines are not the same. It is page 132 -- 131 -- we have different. Yes, 131 goes to 132, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you remember that a few minutes ago I asked you this question: "Did the APCs have weapons, perhaps guns, mounted somewhere on their top?" And you replied "Yes." Do you remember that I asked you that question and you gave me that answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I meant a machine-gun or a small 20-millimetre, which is a small anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: It's not really a proper big gun, a big calibre gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no. But were those weapons ever used, that is, the machine-guns or 20-millimetres that were mounted on the three APCs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were they used against targets on the other side of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: They were used when Muslim units would attack with great force Nedzarici and when in some places they tried to break through the lines, and then they would act under force and necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed because they were armoured, weren't they? They were protected from, at least, small arms fire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: They were not protected from guns which the Muslim army had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: They were protected from small armed forces fire, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, did your duties change at any stage from those you just told us up until August of 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You tell us that sometime in mid-1993 your position was changed from the institute of theology to the Energoinvest building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Where was that building, the Energoinvest building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: The Energoinvest building was at the beginning of the street, at the end of Kasindol Street which leads to Ilidza. If you have a map, I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You mean near your battalion headquarters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the same word was forgotten. I heard from the witness -- I can't say it, but I know that same word was not translated. There's a sign, a cryptogram. It wasn't translated. I will ask for the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... start with the Energoinvest building was ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. I will try to clarify it. Witness you were asked a question where was that building, the Energoinvest building, and then you started your answer by saying the Energoinvest building was at the -- and then could you please repeat what you then said. I think you gave the street ask then said that that street leads to -- could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Energoinvest building is at Ilidza, at the end of Kasindol Street, where the street bordered on Ilidza, the Kasindol Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is what makes it difficult. I am saying that the precise word that was used and that I heard from the mouth of the witness was not repeated. I'll ask for the tape because it's the same word as a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you can demonstrate later on, once you've heard the tape that a word is missing, then we'll take care that the translation will be redacted in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what happened to the APCs once you moved to the Energoinvest building. Did they remain there, or were you allowed to take them out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Mostly all the vehicles while under UNPROFOR control were in a hangar belonging to the Energoinvest company, and an armoured vehicle was left to us which we made out of a small truck and which we continued to use for food delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Does that mean that -- does that mean that from mid-1993 your duties from then on until at least August 1994 were confined to delivering food? That's all you did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "mostly," what else did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: As I said, I pulled out the dead and wounded soldiers of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you continue to do those duties until the end of the war at the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you -- I withdraw that. You told us that there were civilians living in Nedzarici during the war, including your mother. Approximately how many civilians were there living in Nedzarici, say, at the end of 1992? Are we talking about hundreds of civilians or thousands of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Hundreds of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: More than 500?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: More than 100?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Around 100 to 200 civilians lived in Nedzarici during war. It was not a large settlement. It's a settlement with about 1.000 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that no part of Nedzarici was further than, say, a kilometre from the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How far did your mother live from the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: My mother was 200 metres on the outside from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You told us that your mother's house was damaged. Was the roof damaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Partly the roof was hit, but overnight we managed to repair the tiles to keep out the rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the roofs of many of the houses in Nedzarici, especially close to the front line, had extensive roof damage during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why did your mother not leave Nedzarici during the war, given the obvious danger that she was in by remaining there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Because she didn't want to leave me. She only has me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Although she preferred to stay there, do you know whether your superiors felt any responsibility to perhaps move them against their will from positions so close to the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: My mother didn't want to leave her house, and I never discussed the issue with her. I was the one who could have told her to go someplace but she wanted to stay. Normally the superiors and especially the battalion commander told the company commanders that all soldiers who have family in Nedzarici and who know civilians who are not safe, who are in an exposed position, that they should try to protect themselves or to move someplace. It was up to the wish of the people living there. These are people who have been living there for 50, 60, 100 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If I understand what you just said correctly, the battalion commander gave instructions down the line of command to the effect that civilians in a position of danger should either protect themselves or move elsewhere, but some of the people wanted to stay nevertheless; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The same applied for areas close to the front line on the other side of the front line, didn't it? In other words, there were civilians living close to the front line on the other side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why would you assume the position to be any different with people on the other side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when we were speaking about the front line with the witness, we were asked to be precise regarding duration and time. I should like the same to apply now, that is, are we talking about 1992, 1993, or what, whatever? That is our opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a question to which the time issue clearly does not apply with the same strictures as the -- as when the issue arose with questions asked by the Defence to which I objected. But in the interest of saving time, I'm happy to put a time frame on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You've told us that there were around 100 or 200 civilians who remained in Nedzarici during war. Now, I take it that applied between September 1992 and August 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war there were slightly more. So in the period from the beginning of 1992, when war started, that is, April until December 1992, because many civilians were wounded and killed, as I said, and who could no longer be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You remember that I asked you, I think, for the figure as of the end of 1992. Were there 100 to 200 people there, civilians, at the end of 1992, as best as you could estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: There were about 200 civilians in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, why did you not think that the same situation applied to the areas immediately on the other side of the front line between September 1992 and August 1994, that there would be civilians who had lived there for long periods of time who didn't want to leave? Why would you not think the same applied there as on your side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Because I have relatives who lived at Vojnicko Polje and whose apartment was unlivable, and the Muslim army, the Muslim command, would not let them move out. They were living in an apartment that was exposed to Nedzarici. There were buildings on the front line and they were not allowed to move out. And I omitted to say that in Nedzarici, apart from the civilian population - and I only counted people living in homes - there was an old person's home with at least 100 people living there, and that was also on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You see, what you're telling us is that you were aware of, I take it, some civilians, some Serb civilians, who were living on the other side of the confrontation line close to the front line but against their will; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. Well, why would you not assume that apart from them, that particular family, that there would be other civilians living close to the front line, as they were on your side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Because they had plenty of places to go to. There were vacant flats in town that they could go to. But in our -- on our side there wasn't that much free space. The whole of Ilidza was full. There were no empty apartments and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But that wasn't the reason that your mother didn't leave, was it? She wanted to stay; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you ever told by any of your superiors that there were not civilians living on the other side of the front line within a particular depth of the front line? Were you ever told that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, were you ever told by your superiors that there may be civilians living and moving around within, say, a couple of hundred metres of the front line on the other side? Were you ever told that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: We were told that there might be civilians in that settlement coming to their apartments, and I said that the company commander would non-stop repeat that fire should not be opened without necessity if one noticed a civilian, and this was the front line for all of us, for combatants on both sides. It was a zone of high risk. There was just shooting, so a civilian had no -- nothing to do there. I never sent my mother to the front line, nor did she go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I take it there were times that you fired weapons onto the ABiH side between September 1992 and August 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In that period of time, did you ever fire a weapon, you personally, onto the other side of the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I said only under necessity, when there was a major attack by the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you didn't think there were civilians living or around the area close to the front line; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same technique. This question has been put to this witness. He has answered it clearly, and one keeps coming back to it again and again. It's close to harassment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is the question has been answered before and that therefore there would be no need to put it again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It leads to a further point this time round, Mr. President. But I'm happy to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you fired weapons into the ABiH territory, did you allow for the possibility that there were civilians in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: We opened fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you to take off your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question is the very example of an ambush because there's so many circumstances under which one might open fire. Perhaps the witness was attacked. He had to return fire. Maybe he saw a soldier preparing for action. He had to open fire, et cetera. When he's told in such case, did you open fire? Did you know there was a civilian behind? I think one should be precise and one should not make any automatic implication.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It wasn't a leading question, even though it's cross-examination. The witness has already said that he presumed that there were not civilians living in the immediate area of the front line on the other side. It's a fair question. When he fired into ABiH territory, did he allow for the possibility that there were civilians in the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question: When you fired weapons in --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that if we -- if Mr. Ierace is to be heard, the witness should put on his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please put them on. Yes, Mr. Ierace. It has advantages if the witness has his headphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sometimes it has advantages to have them off, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question, if I can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you fired weapons into ABiH territory, did you allow for the possibility that there were civilians in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: At any point of time when a Muslim attack occurred against Nedzarici, if we were opening fire, we took that into consideration. But it was inconceivable to us that there would be anyone on the front line, where combat was ongoing, where there was a separation of some 10 or 15 metres, that there should be any civilians there. Even mice hid in their holes. My mother hid. When I go home, I would hear her say, "When the shooting started, I hid under the bed," things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying that when there was an operation on, when there was a fair degree of military activity on both sides, at those times you would expect civilians to make themselves scarce; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Certainly. If there were any civilians, I would expect them to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might the witness be shown P3279T with the number 9A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, could you give us now an indication how much time you still need, because we have to take into account as well the tapes have to be changed if we go on for too long a time, and whether we'd have another break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage my best estimate would be the best part of an hour. I note there are a number of sniping incidents which have been covered in this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- I'll do some accounting on the time used until now, but let's have a break in approximately five minutes. Could you find a suitable moment for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is this document under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Perhaps the first photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes well, Ms. Pilipovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first we will deal with the photograph and then ask Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There's a sequence of three photographs, Mr. President. It might save time if I give the relevant numbers. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That photograph is not under seal. Part of the same set, I think, is photograph ending with the number 35. If you want to start with that one and then go to 3A might be a better order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like 9A first?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 35 first and then 9A and then -- I'm sorry, 35 first, then 3A, then 9A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, the Defence would just like to draw attention to the fact that the General spent two hours today in a cold room. And in view of his health, we fear that this could have adverse consequences on the proceedings. And also I wish to say that the General did not even have lunch today. So I really don't know about our working hours today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How productive they will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, General Galic, if your health situation would not allow to continue, please inform me. That's, I would say, a standing rule of which I hope you understood it to be consistently in effect. We will have a break, I think, in five minutes. Am I well informed that you did not have any lunch? Then I'll take care that at least there's something during the next break so that you'll not starve in this -- I don't know whether you had any lunch or not, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have lunch, General Galic, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I address you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I spent two hours in a cold room, and I asked for some warmth and the guards tried to help me but they didn't succeed, so I was very cold. Secondly, I haven't had lunch, but I am not that hungry, and I certainly won't starve. And thirdly, I can sustain these additional efforts for as long as is necessary. And especially I'd like to help my soldier to complete his task here today, for him to be able to arrive -- to carry out his obligations in time and also to allow the Court to complete their part of the work. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I indicated before, this is highly appreciated. I'll see to it that at least you'll get a warmer place for the next break. There must be a solution to that. And at least that there would be something to eat. I'll see whether we can manage that. Usually the food is transported from the detention facilities, so there must have been something wrong, or perhaps they were not prepared for you to stay here. But I'll take care that something will be done. Mr. Ierace. Thank you very much, General Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest, Your Honour, that -- I don't want to create any problems regarding the food at all. It's not a problem for me to be in the cell for 20 minutes or half an hour, but if it's two hours then it's a problem. I hope you understand. I tried to make myself very clear. Twenty to 30 minutes is okay, but two hours is a bit too much. I don't want to waste any more of your time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you ever have an afternoon additional hearing, I'll take care that this will not happen again. And I'm learning slowly, as you might have noticed. We highly appreciate your cooperation. Mr. Ierace, if you could find a suitable moment, whether it would be now or soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would be now, Mr. President. And I emphasise that I -- I cannot be confident that I will finish this properly in an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please do your utmost best, because of course I think -- I can imagine that especially if you're coming to the photographs that that's a very relevant issue for the Prosecution. I could have imagined, after what I've heard during the last half an hour, that as far as priority is concerned, that you would have started with that. I'm not the one who should tell you how to cross-examine the witnesses, but I am a bit surprised, and I would really urge you to do this efficiently and as quickly as possible. We'll have a short break, then. I would say that 20 minutes might do. We'll resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I could add that the Prosecution should finish this witness today, Mr. Ierace. I will assist you as good as I can, but under the present circumstances, the Chamber thinks that we should conclude today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hear what you say. I note that the Defence has taken one hour and 44 minutes on our reckoning. So far I've taken 33 minutes. There have been a number of interruptions. Whilst we will do everything we reasonably can to assist the witness, ultimately our primary obligation requires us to seek the opportunity to fairly put all of the relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But I'll do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed of the attention that was paid to your position, General Galic, during the break. I see that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is on his feet. I was informed that Mr. Ierace also would like to address the Chamber. Could you do it quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be all the more faster, since I have no intention to stay here till -- I'm just talking about problems that I have with my laptop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certain that you'll be better assisted by someone else than by the members of this Chamber. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just quickly for the record, firstly the accused in the presence of the witness and looking at the witness said just before the break "I'd like to help my soldier to complete his task here today, for him to be able to arrive -- to carry out his obligations in time and also to allow the Court to complete their part of the work." It was inappropriate for the accused to say that in the presence of the witness, to identify the witness as in the present tense "his soldier." Secondly, in relation to the pressing time constraints on the Prosecution, we'll do our best to assist, but I think it's reached the point where I should make these quick observations. The witness said he's been here 25 days, if that is to believed, because if he's been here 25 days that takes up back to the opening of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he said 21 days but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed it was 21 days, but he said 25 days. Is this an issue that we should at this very moment solve, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, it's relevant in this way -- and I'll just quickly add, if Ms. Pilipovic was concerned about her client not receiving lunch, at the end of cross-examination and early into -- at the end of examination-in-chief was not the time to raise it. It's relevant because of the pressure which the Prosecution -- not just me personally -- is under to deal with six scheduled incidents in an hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll not give any -- I'll not say much on the observations just made by Mr. Ierace, although certainly other words could have been used by General Galic, the Chamber has understood what he said as an expression of specifically -- of understanding what were the reasons why the witness had to go back, and the Chamber therefore -- other words could have been used. The Chamber does not adopt the view of the Prosecution. Let's just continue with the witness, if -- unless there's really something that need attention now, and that's not a response to whether it was the right time or not to talk about food or -- but only the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have to say this: For the Defence, this type of intervention by the Prosecution represents an attempt to destabilise the Defence and the accused and clearly it violate it is principle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, has the response of the Chamber not been clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was crystal clear, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. DP8. Mr. Ierace, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown the map for sniping incident 25 that was shown to the witness by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is D1775.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, on the map in front of you, do you see the number "26" along a dot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Earlier you said that that part of that building could not be seen from positions held by the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In fact I think you said that side of the building, or words to that effect, could not be seen from positions held by the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes. From that side where it says "26," you could not see it from where the Army of Republika Srpska was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please move closer to the microphone when you give your answers to that we can hear you. Now, do you base that on the way the buildings appear on the map, or do you base it on your own observations made from positions of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I am saying on the basis of what I knew at the time when I was in the Army of Republika Srpska, that is, between 1992 to 1994/1995, and I'm saying that one could not see them from any of our positions, any of the positions from which the Army of Republika Srpska operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps that map might be kept close by and in the meantime the witness shown photograph 35. I think it's part of Exhibit P3279T.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the buildings which appear in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you see that in the centre of the photograph, there is a gap between the two high-rise buildings to either side, behind which one can see a third high-rise building filling the gap?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you agree that it's apparent that the photograph was taken from somewhere in Nedzarici, in particular clearly in an area that was occupied by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sorry. I withdraw it, not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: This was not taken from the lines held by the Army of Republika Srpska. This was taken from somewhere in the heart of Nedzarici, that is, 2 or 300 metres away from the city, away from Vojnicko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you accept that it was taken from somewhere in territory held during the war by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must object. After all, when one knows the modern means, that is, the objectives technically, this photograph could have been taken from no matter where. So if the question has to do with the exact location, it cannot be answered because the witness was not there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will ask another question to accommodate my friend's concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you accept the view that this photograph affords of this building is a view one could have had from territory held by the VRS ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Not in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown -- I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the building alongside the number 26 which appeared on the map? Have you ever been to that building or stood outside the front of it or driven past it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I've been looking at those buildings for 20 years, passing by them, entering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Might the witness be shown the photograph ending with the number and letter 9A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, that is a photograph of that building; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you notice that around the entrance which appears at the foot of one of the buildings there appears to be shell damage and small arms fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness now be shown the photograph ending with the number and letter 3A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, this is a photograph taken from one of the top storeys of the building which appeared in the earlier photograph. Do you recognise the institute of theology appearing in the gap between the two buildings in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: I am positive that this is not the same photograph that was shown me a moment ago, and the building for which you said -- and this is not the building that you say was destroyed. I am very well familiar with that area, and I know the position of the buildings and which one faces which. I told you that I've live there had for 20 years and I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your belief. I understand your evidence. Do you identify the institute of theology appearing in the gap between the two high-rise buildings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So witness, the question was whether you recognise in the gap between the buildings, the institute of theology. So forget for a moment -- yes? Your answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The houses in between the high-rise buildings immediately in the front and the institute in the background, they were all on the VRS side of the front line, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: They were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The houses as they appear in this photograph were not -- do not show the condition they were in at any stage during the war, do they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: They don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: This photograph shows this residential area half clearly recent rebuilding, including what appear to be new roofs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: It is. And one can see that the monastery building has been renovated, that is, the building of the school of theology.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. And this photograph also demonstrates the height of the institute compared to the surrounding buildings; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP8
utterances.text: Well, this photograph shows how tall is the building by comparing it with the building that this photograph was taken of, because the building that this photograph was taken from is eight-storeys high and this school of theology three storeys. So one can see how much lower these houses are than the one from which the photograph was taken, and this include it is school of theology.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage might the witness be shown D1764. It's a map. And might the witness be given a ruler.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence proposes to offer its ruler to the Prosecution if the Prosecution will accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm sure it's straight, Mr. President. Might the ELMO focus in on the pen drawings on the map. Perhaps the map might be raised a little. Thank you.
